question: In Tennessee, time-share programs and vacation clubs are primarily regulated under which body of state law?
choice_c: The Tennessee Time-Share Act of 1981, codified at T.C.A. Title 66, Chapter 32, Part 1
explanation: Tennessee time-share programs and vacation clubs are governed by the Tennessee Time-Share Act of 1981, found at T.C.A. Title 66, Chapter 32, Part 1, which sets out definitions, registration, disclosure, and licensing requirements specific to time-share sales.
source_note: T.C.A. Title 66, Chapter 32, Part 1 — Tennessee Time-Share Act of 1981

question: Under the Tennessee Time-Share Act, an "acquisition agent" is best described as a person who does what?
choice_a: Holds title to time-share property on behalf of the developer
choice_b: Manages the day-to-day operations of a time-share resort's homeowners' association
choice_d: Uses means such as telephone, mail, or advertisement to encourage a person to attend a time-share sales presentation
explanation: T.C.A. § 66-32-102 defines an acquisition agent as a person who, by telephone, mail, advertisement, inducement, solicitation, or other means, directly attempts to encourage a person to attend a sales presentation for a time-share program — a distinct role from the salesperson who actually closes the sale.

question: Before receiving an acquisition agent license in Tennessee, an applicant's affiliated broker must certify that the applicant has completed which training requirement?
choice_a: A 30-hour training program covering the fundamentals of the Tennessee Time-Share Act and related topics
choice_d: No training is required if the applicant already holds an affiliate broker license
explanation: Under the Tennessee Time-Share Act, an acquisition agent applicant's sponsoring broker must certify that the applicant completed a 30-hour training program in the fundamentals of the Tennessee Time-Share Act and related subject matter before the commission will issue the license.
source_note: T.C.A. Title 66, Chapter 32, Part 1 — Tennessee Time-Share Act, acquisition agent licensing

question: Under Tennessee law, may a person simultaneously hold an active time-share salesperson license and an active acquisition agent license?
choice_a: Yes — there is no restriction on holding both concurrently
choice_b: No — a person may not hold both licenses active at the same time
choice_c: Yes, but only if the person works for the same time-share developer
choice_d: Yes, but only after five years of combined experience
explanation: The Tennessee Time-Share Act specifically prohibits a person from holding both an active time-share salesperson license and an active acquisition agent license at the same time, keeping the two distinct roles in the time-share sales process separated.
source_note: T.C.A. Title 66, Chapter 32, Part 1 — Tennessee Time-Share Act, license restrictions

question: For a Tennessee real estate licensee who also participates in time-share sales activity, how does a violation of the Tennessee Time-Share Act of 1981 (or its rules) affect their real estate license?
choice_a: It has no bearing whatsoever on the person's real estate broker license
choice_b: It can only be enforced against the time-share developer, never against an individual licensee
choice_c: It can constitute grounds for disciplinary action against the licensee's real estate license under the Tennessee Real Estate Broker License Act
choice_d: It automatically upgrades the licensee's status to principal broker
explanation: Tennessee licensing law treats a violation of the Tennessee Time-Share Act of 1981 or its implementing rules as a disciplinable offense that the Tennessee Real Estate Commission may act on against the individual's real estate license, in addition to any time-share-specific consequences.
source_note: T.C.A. Title 62, Chapter 13 (Tennessee Real Estate Broker License Act) cross-referenced with the Tennessee Time-Share Act of 1981

question: Under T.C.A. § 62-13-104, a resident manager who is an employee of a broker or an owner and manages an apartment building, duplex, or residential complex is exempt from real estate licensure only if the manager's duties are limited to which activities?
choice_a: Any activity at all, including negotiating and signing new leases on the owner's behalf
choice_b: Only mowing the lawn and performing minor repairs
choice_c: Selling the property on the owner's behalf without a license
choice_d: Supervision of the property, exhibiting units, and leasing or collecting security deposits and rentals — without negotiating the amount of rent, deposits, or lease terms
explanation: T.C.A. § 62-13-104 exempts a resident manager whose duties are limited to supervising the property, exhibiting units, and collecting rents and deposits, from real estate licensure — but only so long as that person does not negotiate the amount of rent, security deposits, or the terms of any lease, which would require a license.

question: A Tennessee property management company collects rent and negotiates lease renewal terms for multiple property owners in exchange for a management fee. What licensing status generally applies to this activity?
choice_a: A real estate broker license is generally required, because the company is negotiating leases and collecting rent for others for compensation, beyond the narrow resident-manager exemption
choice_b: No license is ever required for any form of third-party property management in Tennessee
choice_c: Only a business license from the local county clerk is required
choice_d: A license is required only if the properties are commercial, never for residential rentals
explanation: Because the narrow exemption in T.C.A. § 62-13-104 covers only a resident/on-site manager who does not negotiate rent or lease terms, a property management company that negotiates leases and collects rent for compensation on behalf of multiple owners falls squarely within activity requiring a Tennessee real estate broker license.
source_note: T.C.A. § 62-13-104 and T.C.A. § 62-13-102 — Tennessee Real Estate Broker License Act, licensable activity

question: Under TREC Rule 1260-02-.09, when a principal broker's firm manages rental properties and collects security deposits and rents on behalf of owners, how must those funds generally be held?
choice_a: In the principal broker's personal checking account, for convenience
choice_b: In a separate escrow or trustee account maintained by the principal broker, distinct from the firm's operating account, and not commingled with the broker's own funds
choice_c: In cash, kept in a locked drawer at the brokerage office
choice_d: There is no requirement to segregate property management trust funds from brokerage operating funds
explanation: TREC Rule 1260-02-.09 requires each principal broker to maintain a separate escrow or trustee account for trust money received in a fiduciary capacity — which includes rents and security deposits collected on behalf of owners in a property management arrangement — and expressly prohibits commingling those funds with the firm's own operating funds.
source_note: TREC Rule 1260-02-.09 — Managing escrow or trustee accounts

question: Under TREC Rule 1260-02-.09, when an affiliate broker managing rental property on behalf of a principal broker's firm receives trust money (such as a tenant's rent payment or security deposit), what must the affiliate broker do?
choice_a: Deposit the funds into the affiliate broker's own personal account and reconcile at year-end
choice_b: Hold the funds indefinitely until the tenant moves out
choice_c: Pay the trust money over to the principal broker immediately upon receipt
choice_d: Use the funds to cover the affiliate broker's own commission first, then remit the balance
explanation: TREC Rule 1260-02-.09 requires an affiliate broker to pay over to the principal broker with whom the affiliate is affiliated all trust money — including funds collected in a property management context — immediately upon receipt, so that it can be properly deposited into the firm's escrow/trustee account.
source_note: TREC Rule 1260-02-.09 — Managing escrow or trustee accounts, affiliate broker duties

question: Under Tennessee real estate agency disclosure law, the written agency disclosure requirements of T.C.A. §§ 62-13-403 through 62-13-405 generally do NOT apply to which type of transaction, relevant to commercial and industrial brokerage practice?
choice_a: The sale of a single-family owner-occupied residence
choice_b: The sale of a condominium unit
choice_c: The sale of a mobile home on a permanent foundation
choice_d: The sale, lease, or transfer of commercial property
explanation: T.C.A. § 62-13-405 exempts several categories of transactions from the written agency disclosure requirements, including transactions involving commercial property, property transferred by public auction, residential property of more than four units, and the lease or rental of residential property.
source_note: T.C.A. § 62-13-405 — Written disclosure, exemptions for commercial transactions

question: Under T.C.A. § 62-13-104, a corporation that owns commercial or industrial real estate may have one of its own officers handle the management, lease, or sale of that property without the officer holding a real estate broker license, subject to which limitation?
choice_a: The exemption applies only when the transaction is incident to managing property the corporation itself owns, and does not extend to compensation that is dependent upon or related to the value of the real estate
choice_b: The exemption has no limitations and covers any real estate activity performed by any corporate employee
choice_c: The exemption applies equally to LLCs, LLPs, and partnerships acting through any member
choice_d: The exemption only applies if the officer is also a licensed attorney
explanation: T.C.A. § 62-13-104 exempts a corporation acting through a duly authorized officer from broker licensure for transactions incident to managing, leasing, selling, or otherwise disposing of real estate the corporation itself owns — but this exemption does not cover a person whose compensation depends on the value of the real estate, and by its terms does not extend to LLCs or partnerships.
source_note: T.C.A. § 62-13-104 — Exemptions, corporate officer handling company-owned real estate

question: Because commercial and industrial real estate transactions in Tennessee can sometimes be handled by an owner's own corporate officer under the T.C.A. § 62-13-104 exemption, what must a broker evaluating a similar arrangement carefully verify?
choice_a: Whether the property is located inside city limits
choice_b: Whether the person's compensation is tied to the value of the real estate or is otherwise structured in a way that falls outside the narrow exemption and instead requires a real estate license
choice_c: Whether the transaction involves more than $1,000,000 in value
choice_d: Nothing; all commercial real estate activity in Tennessee is automatically license-exempt
explanation: Because the corporate-officer exemption under T.C.A. § 62-13-104 is narrowly limited to non-value-based compensation for managing the corporation's own property, a broker or the commission must scrutinize the compensation structure and scope of activity to determine whether the exemption genuinely applies or whether licensable brokerage activity is actually occurring.
source_note: T.C.A. § 62-13-104 — Exemptions, scope limitations relevant to commercial/industrial practice
